TINGSHU WANG/REUTERS   Earlier this year, I put a blunt question to an adviser to China’s central bank: With the property bust grinding into its fourth year, how likely was it that the country’s strained financial system would finally crack into a full-blown crisis?

   It depends, the adviser said, on your definition of a financial crisis. By some Western yardsticks, he suggested, China had arguably had several already.

   I thought about that conversation again this month, when Beijing announced it would pump roughly 360 billion yuan , about $54 billion, into some of its largest banks and insurers. What struck me was that instead of flowing to the weakest ones, the money is being funneled into the system’s strongest institutions, like the Industrial & Commercial Bank of China and China Life Insurance. And when the plan was unveiled, bank and insurer shares in China fell rather than rose.

   To understand why a rescue of the seemingly healthy would unsettle investors, I went to Michael Pettis, the former Peking University finance professor who has spent years arguing that China’s balance sheets don’t work the way outsiders assume. Pettis is now writing a book on this topic.

   His starting point upends the usual China-debt story. “Banking crises are not caused by high levels of debt,” he told me, “but rather by asset-liability mismatches.” In a system like China’s, which features a closed capital account, state-owned banks and a large and captive pool of household deposits, regulators can restructure those mismatches almost at will, Pettis explained. That shifts losses around the financial system and compels banks to roll over loans. A sudden liquidity panic, the kind that felled Lehman Brothers, he noted, is something Beijing can nearly always head off.

   But, Pettis said, “it’s a mistake to think that the real cost of a debt problem lies in the possibility of a financial crisis.” Resolving a severe debt problem slowly, he argued, can prove far more expensive over time than resolving it quickly through a crisis. 

   In other words, a crisis, for all its violence, clears the books. The slow path does not.

   So what is this month’s recapitalization? It’s a way to buy time, in Pettis’s telling. It “strengthens the banks’ capital buffers while giving the authorities more time to deal with losses and declining returns without forcing an immediate recognition and liquidation,” he said. 

   Still, the losses don’t vanish. “Ultimately,” he said, “the losses must still be absorbed somewhere in the economy through higher taxes, lower returns to households … or some combination of these.”

   That is the line ordinary Chinese should watch most closely, because for years they have been the ones footing the bill. Low deposit rates transferred income from savers to borrowers—a reasonable trade when China was capital-poor and investment paid off. It’s a worse trade now. With returns falling, the same machinery increasingly funds unproductive projects and rolls over bad debt rather than generating new wealth.

   And the machinery is under visible strain: banks’ net interest margins—the gap between what they earn on loans and pay out on deposits—have sunk to record lows, leaving less room to absorb the next round of losses.

   Topping up the banks’ capital, as Pettis puts it, “doesn’t create real economic wealth.” Sooner or later Beijing confronts a narrower path, he added: write down the bad investments, absorb the losses through the budget, or shift more income back to households and lean less on investment to drive growth.

   An elusive economic drag   There is a subtler cost, too. As households and companies sense the losses drifting toward them, they spend less and invest less. Economists like Pettis call these financial-distress costs. China’s famously reluctant consumers are already living with them.

   Does the slow-motion version ever tip into outright panic? I asked Pettis what would change his mind about that. His base case, he said, looks more like Japan’s lost decades: a long stretch in which bad investments are rolled over, losses are socialized, and growth gradually erodes. He considers a Lehman-style rupture unlikely, because Beijing doesn’t depend on willing private creditors. It can force the rollovers itself.

   He listed the signals he would watch for: a genuine domestic run on the banks, capital outflows accelerating beyond Beijing’s ability to contain them, or the failure of a major institution that the government chose not to rescue. None, he said, looks likely in the next few years.

   Which brings me back to my central-bank adviser and his answer about definitions. Perhaps the most Chinese feature of a Chinese financial crisis is that there may never be a single moment we can point to and call the crisis. Beijing has grown adept at keeping a crisis from ever coming to a head, and this recapitalization is the latest example.

   It’s also a reminder of its limit. As Pettis told me, the system can make a Western-style financial crisis less likely without making the underlying problem any less costly.

   If a Chinese financial crisis never produces a single dramatic moment, how will we know it happened—and does it make it easier for Beijing to manage, or easier for everyone else to ignore? This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

China in a Few Headlines

 

• Mounting geopolitical uncertainty with the U.S. has prompted China and India to ease diplomatic tensions and loosen investment restrictions.

 

• After eight years, Huawei is on trial in Brooklyn over U.S. trade secret and fraud charges, which the tech giant vigorously denies.

 

• China’s economic troubles reach the mushroom hunters of Shangri-La.

 

• Chinese biotechs are going global with GLP-1 weight-loss drugs to escape low domestic margins.

 
 
 

The Number

 
$4.5 million
 

Crypto billionaire Justin Sun has hired a celebrity lawyer to sue actress Jing Tian for $4.5 million after their rumored marriage plans fizzled out.

 
 
 

A Closer Look

 
 
 
 

U.S. intelligence agencies have formally accused six Chinese AI firms—including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba—of executing industrial-scale “distillation” campaigns to extract capabilities from leading American AI models like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok.

 
 
 

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked how the U.S. should think about China—as a rising great power, a totalitarian state, or something else. Readers shared their thoughts:. Readers shared their thoughts:

 

“Xi Jinping’s consolidation of power over the party and the government represents a complete break with the previous regime. He is a Marxist-Leninist who revitalized ties with Vladimir Putin and declared at Moscow’s airport, at the end of a visit, that changes were occurring in the world ‘the likes of which we haven’t seen in 100 years—and we are the ones driving these changes together.’ His is a vision for turning every point of contact with the West into an ideological combat zone.”—Bill Holstein, New York

 

“Having spent three decades engaged in business development as a U.S. tech-company representative trying to do business with China, I’ve been continually challenged with how to understand and work with my China counterparts. While hitting China with tariffs is necessary in the short term, the strategy will fail unless and until the U.S. can focus on the creation of growth areas in which we have substantial long-term advantages and coordinate labor with private businesses and government policy to dominate these sectors globally.”— Dave Vieau (former CEO of A123 Systems), Rhode Island

 

“China is an absolutely totalitarian state. How can one think otherwise when seeing the level of control over any independent (i.e. diverging from official views) information or opinion, written or not. For third parties—Western or not—dealing with such a country can no longer be a normal transaction because it’s impossible to trust any interlocutor, since everyone is constantly under state or party surveillance and behaves as such. Furthermore it’s obvious that the Chinese state’s behavior internationally shows that it’s using every means, except direct military aggression, to weaken other countries. It would be tragic for the world if American decision makers have not all understood this and adapted their strategy accordingly.” — Luc Malâtre, France

 

(Responses have been condensed and edited.)

 
 
 

A Name in the News

 
 
Min Zin, wearing a checked shirt, at the base of the Golden State Bridge.
 

The U.S. has designated Myanmar scholar and American citizen Min Zin as wrongfully detained following his arrest in China on espionage charges, framing his case for upcoming high-level bilateral talks.
